fixes.find: City & Suburban treats a commercial no-heat call as priority work, with same-day service when the schedule allows. Where a landlord supplies the heat, the Chicago Heat Ordinance sets a general rule from September 15 to June 1. The minimum is 68 degrees from 8:30 a.m. to 10:30 p.m. and 66 degrees overnight (Chicago Municipal Code 13-196-410). The code lists exceptions. Where the same system also heats apartments above the shop, the dwelling units carry the ordinance minimums. The repair therefore has a legal deadline attached to the residential space.
fixes.replace: City & Suburban offers same-day service when the schedule allows and emergency HVAC service every day till midnight, except Sundays; maintenance plan members get priority dispatch. The Chicago Heat Ordinance sets minimums for dwelling units, not a blanket temperature for commercial-only space. Where the same system also heats apartments above the shop and the landlord supplies that heat, those units must reach 68 degrees from 8:30 a.m. to 10:30 p.m. and 66 degrees overnight from September 15 to June 1 (Chicago Municipal Code 13-196-410), subject to the code's exceptions. That puts a legal minimum on the residential space.
fixes.why: CRITICAL 1: unconditional commercial no-heat priority removed (only member priority dispatch is approved); Rule 4: Heat Ordinance scoped to dwelling units

fixes.find: Four checks are safe for staff and often shorten the visit. Confirm the thermostat is calling for heat or cool, not fan only. Look for a tripped breaker. Check whether a service switch near the furnace or air handler was flipped off. Pull the filter and see whether it is packed with dust. Anything past that is technician work: opening a gas-fired unit, repeatedly resetting a locked-out control, or climbing onto a roof. A smell of gas is a different call, to the utility and the fire department first. City & Suburban diagnoses before quoting, and those four answers give the technician a head start.
fixes.replace: A gas smell, smoke or a carbon monoxide alarm comes first: everyone leaves the building and calls 911, or the gas utility for a gas odor, from outside. Otherwise, four checks are reasonable for staff. Confirm the thermostat is calling for heat or cool, not fan only. Look for a tripped breaker. Check whether a service switch near the furnace or air handler was flipped off. Where the filter sits in an accessible indoor slot, shut the system off as the manufacturer directs before checking whether it is packed with dust. Anything past that is technician work: opening energized or gas-fired equipment, repeatedly resetting a locked-out control, or going onto a roof. City & Suburban diagnoses before quoting, and those answers give the technician a head start.
fixes.why: MAJOR 4 + safety rule 3: evacuate-and-call first; filter check only after manufacturer-safe shutdown at an accessible filter; no energized equipment or roof access

fixes.find: Emergency and routine commercial HVAC repairs follow four visit steps. The technician confirms the complaint with the person who reported it. The equipment and its controls are inspected, and electrical and refrigerant values measured. The failure and the price are named before work starts. A repair that needs no ordered part is usually finished in the first visit; City & Suburban names the expected sequence at the quote rather than afterward.
fixes.replace: Emergency and routine commercial HVAC repairs usually follow four steps. The complaint is confirmed with the person who reported it. The equipment and its controls are inspected, with electrical and refrigerant values measured where the fault calls for it. City & Suburban diagnoses the failure and puts the price in writing before work starts. A repair that needs no ordered part can often be finished in the first visit, depending on access and the fault. The quote is the place to ask for the expected sequence.
